\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Randomised experiments on a social or marketplace network violate the assumption that one unit's outcome does not depend on another's assignment, and the quantity of interest is usually the \emph{global average treatment effect} (GATE): the difference in mean outcome if every unit were treated rather than none.
Difference in means (DM) is biased for it; design-based estimators with an exposure mapping \citep{aronow2017estimating,ugander2013graph,eckles2017design} are unbiased only if the mapping is right, and weight the few units whose exposure is extreme.
\emph{Regression adjustment} \citep{chin2019regression,han2023model} avoids both: fit the outcome on the unit's own treatment and graph-based exposure covariates such as the treated fraction of its neighbours, then predict at the all-treated and all-control assignments and difference the predictions. It uses every unit and needs no weights.

How well it works, what governs its error and when it fails is not known.
The estimator fits a model where exposures occur and evaluates it where they do not: under Bernoulli($p$) assignment a unit with $d$ neighbours sees a treated fraction concentrated around $p$ with spread $\sqrt{p(1-p)/d}$, and the two global corners, fraction $1$ and fraction $0$, lie far outside it.
\citet{chin2019regression} points this out qualitatively and draws the analogy to off-policy evaluation.
We take it as the organising idea, not as a novelty, and ask what it predicts and whether the predictions hold.
Our reading is that the error has two parts with different drivers: the \emph{variance} is the leverage of the corner contrast in the regression, which grows with degree; the \emph{bias} is the response's curvature times the raw distance from the observed exposures to the corner, which does not grow with degree for a smooth response and which no regression can estimate from data that never visit the corner.

Randomised experiments on networks suffer from interference. A standard estimator of the global average treatment effect (GATE) regresses the outcome on own

shown.message:
P6 is now in the paper and pushed to `dev` as 2ec05c1. The main text is still nine pages, with References starting on page 10 and no undefined references in my local build.

- **Section 5.4:** one paragraph reports the bound-widened interval on the 666 new cells.
  - It covers 0.99 of cells, against 0.70 for the standard HC0 interval at the same 90% level.
  - It does so at 8–14 times HC0's width, and no better than HC0 widened to the same width (coverage difference −0.010, interval [−0.020, −0.002] over groups).
  - On the threshold mechanism, where we expected it to stay below nominal, it covers 0.998 of 27 cells. That prediction failed, and the paragraph says so.
- **Appendix:** a new paragraph gives the construction and everything else. The multiplier κ̂ was frozen at 0.25, the floor of its grid, so the bound is a bound and not a calibration.
- **Abstract and Discussion:** one clause each says the interval covers only by being wide. I added the Armstrong–Kolesár paper to `refs.bib`. I confirmed it by search; the volume and page numbers are from memory.
- **Cuts:** to hold nine pages I removed the per-family coverage sentence, the Discussion's "Design" limitation (the K=30 truncation is still stated in the Fig. 1 caption and the appendix), the "flexible learners use fixed tunings" limitation, and a few clauses elsewhere.

I asked `experiment-repo` in `paper-repo`#4 to check each P6 number against its code. Two things in that request need an answer:

- **HC0 coverage:** I used the cell-weighted 0.70. The pass-rule file gives a group mean of 0.747.
- **Rank correlation:** its comment says 0.28–0.36, while the CSV shows 0.314 for one case.

I also asked `figtab-repo` in its #4 for an appendix figure showing coverage and width by |bias|/SD stratum, since the main text has no room for it.

Still waiting on `gnn_cells.csv`. Once it lands I'll update the two "graph neural networks not run" sentences and then prepare the `release` pull request.
